value: Does enhancing the reasoning ability of LLM-driven agents make their ultimatum-game behaviour more human-like, or does it instead push them toward the theoretically rational but descriptively unrealistic solution?

By varying only reasoning-related prompting (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought) across GPT models in a one-shot ultimatum game, the study shows that stronger agent reasoning moves simulated behaviour toward the game-theoretic equilibrium and away from real human experimental data.

value: The authors conclude that LLM agents do not spontaneously behave like humans in economic games without prompts carrying social context, so using LLM-driven multi-agent simulations as substitutes for real human groups is currently unwarranted.
quote: Our findings indicate that LLMs, even when endowed with advanced reasoning capabilities, do not naturally exhibit human-like economic behavior unless explicitly guided by prompts that incorporate social context. Consequently, using LLMdriven MAS as stand-ins for real human groups is currently unwarranted.

Building on the findings of Kitadai et al. (2023), we aimed to isolate the impact of reasoning ability by deliberately excluding persona settings, including demographic attributes such as age, gender, and personality.
All prompts were written in English. This choice was made because of known reductions in LLMs performance when prompts are written in languages other than English (Etxaniz et al. 2024).
The simulation strategy involved generating 1000 independent decisions for each unique combination of role (proposer/responder), prompt type, and temperature.
For few-shot prompting, we used 10 data points selected from the raw data in Lin et al. (2020).
